paras: The killing of William Arterberry was the shooting of a prisoner by a band of masked, armed men calling themselves "Vigilants" at Harrison, Boone County, Arkansas, on a Friday night in October 1880. Arterberry, suspected of setting fires in the town, was taken from the guards the sheriff had assigned him and shot dead. The local Harrison Times condemned the killing, and the story circulated in Arkansas papers and as far as Georgia.

Harrison had no apparatus for putting out fires, and several fires thought to be incendiary had alarmed its residents, prompting a public meeting about buying a fire engine. Arterberry had been arrested on suspicion; the Columbus Daily Times said there was no evidence against him and that he was held because he "had a hand in most of the deviltry in Harrison." The Russellville Democrat, summarizing the Harrison Times, called him "a notorious character" suspected of incendiarism and other crimes, and the Harrison Times noted he had been charged with murder in Marion County several years earlier.

According to the Columbus account, a speaker at the fire-engine meeting said that "a cheap plan of protecting the village" was about to be tried, which listeners took to mean the prisoner would be lynched.

As the guards later told the Harrison Times, they and the prisoner had eaten supper at the Miles hotel and were walking back downtown when mounted men halted and surrounded them opposite the old parsonage. The guards drew their weapons but were overpowered: one had a blanket thrown over his head, another had a cocked pistol forced into his mouth, and a third was knocked down. The men marched Arterberry off, apparently to hang him, but he nearly got away and was shot many times, all but one ball entering his back and one striking the center of his forehead.

Between 8 and 9 o'clock, the Times correspondent heard heavy firing near the public square and went with Marshal I. R. Moore to the open place on Stephenson avenue, where Moore's son Bob and Geo. Cotten were standing over the body. A card on the dead man's breast read "Outlaws Take Warning!!" and warned against burning, pistol shooting and selling liquor without a license, signed "VIGILANTS."

The guards said the attackers were all "masked or blacked" and spoke little, so no one was recognized. Some in Harrison suggested the men came partly from Marion County, while others thought local citizens alarmed for public buildings had formed the organization. No report of an inquest, arrests or prosecution appears in the coverage.

The Harrison Times called the affair "a terrible one," said it would "add another blot to our already darkened reputation," and argued that the man "could have been better punished in a legal manner." The Russellville Democrat passed on that condemnation on October 28, and the Sharp County Record reprinted the full account under the headline "The Vigilants at Harrison" on November 4.

The Columbia Banner treated the killing with sarcasm, writing that "Boone county had a little fun last week," stating as fact that Arterberry had set the county jail on fire, and proposing that the seventy-five men be jailed, tried and hanged for murder. In Georgia, the Columbus Daily Times retold the episode on November 24 as a lesson about a town without fire protection, ending with the prisoner fighting "courageously" until his captors, "unable to adjust the noose, shot him to death." None of the papers stated Arterberry's race.

The Columbus Daily Times said the sheriff was hurrying the prisoner by wagon to a safer place when the mob waylaid them, whereas the guards quoted in the Harrison Times described being stopped on foot after supper. The local account, which relays the guards themselves, is the closer source. The accounts also differ on the accusation, from suspicion without evidence in the Columbus paper to the Columbia Banner's flat statement that he burned the jail.

bases: Masked, armed men signing themselves 'Vigilants' overpowered the sheriff's guards, seized the prisoner Arterberry and shot him dead (A3, A2, A5, A7).

A band reported at seventy-five armed men took an arrested prisoner from his guards and shot him, leaving a card warning against burning, shooting and illegal liquor sales, i.e. acting as self-appointed punishers of suspected crime (A2, A3, A5, A7). The papers do not state Arterberry's race.

The Harrison Times account (A3, summarized in A2), the Columbia Banner brief (A5) and the Columbus Daily Times paragraph (A7) agree that a mob took the prisoner from custody and killed him, though A2 and A5 may derive from the Harrison Times.

framing.detail: The Harrison Times called the affair 'a terrible one' that would 'add another blot to our already darkened reputation' and preferred legal punishment.
The Columbia Banner opened with 'Boone county had a little fun last week' and proposed jailing, trying and hanging the seventy-five for murder.
The Columbus Daily Times framed the killing as a 'cheap plan of protecting the village' in a town with no fire apparatus, noting the arrest had no evidence behind it.
